transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Yeah… so, I guess what brings me in is that I started trying to eat cleaner, mostly because I’m trying to get on the lieutenant track and I wanted to be in better shape, more disciplined, you know? At first it felt like a normal thing — cutting out junk, watching portions, being more serious about fitness.

But it’s kind of gotten away from me. Like on shift days, when I know I’m moving all day and burning a lot, I’ll still end up having basically black coffee, maybe a protein shake, and then just a small dinner. And part of me knows that’s not really enough, especially for the job, but I keep doing it. It’s hard to explain without sounding dramatic, but it started as “cleaning things up” and now it feels like I’m cutting meals down more and more.
Do you find yourself afraid of gaining weight or feeling like you need to lose more weight, even if others might say you’re already at a healthy weight?

Yeah… I mean, yes, I do. I don’t like admitting it that way because it sounds kind of vain or irrational, but if the scale is up even one pound, I feel it immediately. Like if we had a big station meal, or I drank a bunch of water late, I can know logically that it’s not real weight or whatever, but I still get this tight feeling in my chest, like I messed up.

And then my mind goes straight to, “Okay, you’re getting soft, you’re slipping, people are going to notice.” Especially at work, I think there’s this pressure — maybe some of it is in my head — that you’re supposed to look controlled and capable. So if the number is higher, even a little, it feels like I’ve blown it somehow, like I’m out of control. I don’t know if I’d say I always think I need to lose more, but I definitely feel like I can’t let it go up.
After eating, do you ever feel the need to exercise excessively, make yourself vomit, or use laxatives or diet pills to compensate for what you’ve eaten?

I don’t really know how to answer that cleanly. I mean… I wouldn’t say I have a specific thing like, “I ate this, now I have to do that,” if that’s what you mean. I don’t make myself throw up or anything like that, and I’m not sitting there with some exact formula in my head after every meal.

Exercise is tricky, though, because with my job and training it’s already part of my life, so it can be hard for me to tell what’s normal and what’s me trying to make up for eating. Like if I feel like I overdid it, I might want to move more or be more strict the next day, but I don’t know if I’d call it “excessive” exactly. Maybe other people would see it differently, I’m not sure.

As far as laxatives or diet pills… no, that’s not really been my thing. Mostly it’s more like I get in my head about what I ate and then I try to tighten things up afterward, but I’m not sure if that counts as compensating the way you mean.
Has your concern about food, weight, or shape started to interfere with your job, relationships, or other areas of your life?

Yeah… I mean, I’m still doing my job. I don’t want to make it sound like I’m missing calls or not pulling my weight or anything, because I’m not. I’m showing up, I’m doing what I’m supposed to do.

But socially at the station, it’s definitely changed. The meals are a big thing there, like everybody eating together, someone making a big pot of something, or the crew ordering food after a rough shift. I used to be right in the middle of that, joking around, sitting with everybody. Now I’ll kind of find reasons not to be there. Like I’ll say I already ate, or I need to check something, or I’ll just hang back and make my own thing separately.

And I know that probably sounds small, but in that job, eating together is kind of part of being part of the crew. So I’ve noticed I’m more off by myself than I used to be. I don’t think anyone’s called me out directly, but I can feel that I’m less… connected, I guess. Like I’m still there physically, still working, but I’m not as much part of the team in those moments because I’m worried about the food.
Have your concerns about food, weight, or shape affected any personal relationships or other areas of your life outside of work, like family time or hobbies?

I’m not totally sure how to answer that. I don’t think it’s caused, like, a huge blowup with my family or anything. Nobody has sat me down and said, “You’re ruining family time,” or something that clear.

But… I guess outside of work I do think about it more than I want to admit. Like if there’s some family dinner or people want to go out, I can get kind of tense beforehand, more than I think I used to. I’ll be thinking about what food is going to be there or whether I’m going to feel uncomfortable afterward, and then I’m not really fully present. I can still show up and act normal, but in my head I’m kind of doing all this calculating and worrying.

With hobbies, I don’t know. I mean, a lot of what I do is already pretty physical, so it gets hard to separate what’s a hobby, what’s just staying fit, and what’s me being weird about my body. I don’t want to overstate it. I still see people, I still do things. It’s just maybe less spontaneous than it used to be. Food being involved can make me hesitate, I guess. But I don’t know if I’d say it’s damaged relationships exactly. It’s more like it takes up space in my head when I’m supposed to be enjoying people.
Do you feel like you are overweight or need to lose weight, even when other people might tell you that you look fine or are already at a healthy weight?

Yeah… I mean, I don’t know if I’d say I walk around thinking, “I’m overweight,” exactly. That word feels kind of too blunt, or maybe I don’t want to admit it that way. But I definitely look at myself like there’s something that needs tightening up, if that makes sense.

Like before work, especially, I’ll catch myself checking in the mirror more than I probably should. Not even the whole body sometimes — it’s specific things, like whether my waist looks lean enough, or whether my face looks… sharp, I guess. If my face looks fuller to me, or my waist doesn’t look the way I think it should, it can throw me off more than I want to admit.

And logically, if someone says I look fine, or that I’m fit, I can hear that. I’m not arguing with them out loud. But it doesn’t always land. Because in my head, especially going into a shift, I feel like I’m supposed to look a certain way — capable, squared away, ready. And if I don’t feel like my body looks that way, it messes with my confidence. Like I don’t feel as command-ready, even if nothing about my actual ability has changed.

So… yeah, I guess other people might say I’m fine, but I don’t always feel fine when I look at myself.

Outside of the changes you’ve described at work and around meals, do your concerns about eating, weight, or shape cause you noticeable distress or interfere with your ability to function in any other important areas of your life, like personal goals, self-esteem, or how you see yourself overall?

Yeah… I think it does, in that way. Maybe not like I can’t get out of bed or I can’t do my job, but it definitely affects how I see myself.

The clearest example is before work. I’ll be getting ready and I’ll look in the mirror, and it’s not just like, “Do I look presentable?” It turns into this whole check of whether my waist looks lean enough, or whether my face looks sharp enough. And if it doesn’t look right to me, even if nothing has actually changed from the day before, it can kind of set the tone for the whole day.

It’s hard to explain without sounding vain, because I know that’s probably how it comes off. But it’s less like I’m trying to look good for attention and more like… I need to feel squared away. Like if my body looks a certain way, then I feel more capable, more in control, more ready to lead or make decisions or just be trusted on shift. And if I look in the mirror and my face seems fuller or my waist doesn’t look how I want, I don’t feel as confident. I start feeling like I’m not as command-ready, even though logically I know my ability to do the job hasn’t changed.

So yeah, I’d say it hits my self-esteem. Maybe more than I like admitting. It’s like my brain uses how I look that morning as a measure of whether I’m okay overall, and that can mess with me.
Do you feel like your body weight or shape influences how you see yourself overall, even when others might not notice anything different or be concerned about it?

Yeah… I think it does. I don’t love saying that, because it sounds like I’m making my whole identity about how I look, and I don’t think that’s exactly it. But if I’m being honest, my weight or shape — or really how I perceive it that day — can affect how I see myself overall.

It’s usually most obvious before work. I’ll be in the mirror getting ready, and instead of just checking that I’m clean and put together, I start zeroing in on specific things. Like, does my waist look lean enough, does my face look sharp enough, do I look… I don’t know, squared away. And if something looks off to me, even something nobody else would notice or care about, it can really mess with my head.

I can go from feeling okay to feeling less confident, like I’m not as prepared or not as command-ready that day. Which I know doesn’t really make sense, because my ability to do the job hasn’t changed because my face looks a little fuller to me in the mirror. But emotionally it still lands that way. It’s like if my body doesn’t look the way I think it should, I feel less solid as a person, or less capable.

So yeah, even if other people aren’t noticing anything, I notice it, or I think I notice it, and then it kind of colors how I feel about myself for the day.
Do you find that your concerns about eating or your body are mainly about a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even if you don’t necessarily feel overweight right now?

Yeah… I think that’s probably the core of it, even if I don’t always say it to myself that clearly.

It’s not always like I’m walking around thinking, “I’m fat right now.” Sometimes it’s more this fear that I’m about to lose control of it, or that one meal is going to push me in the wrong direction. Like at the station, if we have a bigger meal — you know, the kind where everyone’s eating together and it’s heavier food, or I drink more water than usual — and then the scale is up even a pound afterward, my brain reacts like it means something huge.

Logically I know a pound can be water or food or whatever. I do know that. But in the moment, I get this tight feeling, almost like panic in my chest and stomach, like, “I’ve blown it.” Like I messed up and now it’s going to show. And then it’s not just about the number, it turns into this whole thing of imagining people seeing me as soft, or like I don’t have control over myself.

That word “fat” is hard for me to say about myself, but yeah, the fear is there. Fear of gaining, fear of looking less lean, fear that if the number moves up it means I’m slipping. Even if nothing actually looks different to anyone else.
Are you intentionally restricting how much food you eat, even when you feel hungry, because of concerns about your weight or shape?

Yeah… yes. I mean, that’s probably the most honest answer.

It started out feeling more reasonable than it probably is now. Like I told myself I was just eating cleaner, being disciplined, trying to stay lean and ready, especially with trying to move toward the lieutenant track. In my head it was tied to being professional and squared away, not just appearance. But over time it’s turned into me cutting things down a lot more than I think I want to admit.

Like there are shift days where I know, objectively, I’ve burned a lot. We’re moving, training, calls, hauling gear, whatever it is. And I’ll still keep it to black coffee in the morning, maybe a protein shake, and then a small dinner later. And I’ll feel hungry, yeah. I’ll feel it. I’m not confused about whether I’m hungry. I just kind of override it because eating more makes me anxious about my weight or how I’ll look.

I’ll tell myself, “You don’t need that much,” or “Just wait until later,” or “You’ll feel better if you keep it tight today.” And sometimes it does feel better mentally for a little while, like I stayed in control. But I also know it’s not really matching what my body probably needs, especially on work days. So… yeah, I am restricting on purpose. I don’t like saying it that directly, but that’s what it is.

But in the moment, I get this tight feeling, almost like panic in my chest and stomach, like, “I’ve blown it.” Like I messed up and now it’s going to show. And then it’s not just about the number, it turns into this whole thing of imagining people seeing me as soft, or like I don’t have control over myself.

That word “fat” is hard for me to say about myself, but yeah, the fear is there. Fear of gaining, fear of looking less lean, fear that if the number moves up it means I’m slipping. Even if nothing actually looks different to anyone else.

inference.note: The patient's concerns about weight gain, body shape, and the impact on self-esteem and daily functioning align with features of both Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0) and Eating Disorder Not Otherwise Specified (F50.2). The absence of significant weight loss or underweight status and lack of compensatory behaviors like purging make Anorexia Nervosa less likely, but the severity of preoccupation with shape/weight and functional impairment supports continued consideration of F50.0. F50.2 remains as a broader category that captures disordered eating with significant distress and impairment without meeting full criteria for Anorexia Nervosa.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's concerns about food, weight, or shape are driving significantly restrictive eating behaviors, which would help differentiate between Anorexia Nervosa (F50.0) and Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F50.2).
doctor.question: Are you intentionally restricting how much food you eat, even when you feel hungry, because of concerns about your weight or shape?

target_item.name: Restrictive_Intake
target_item.manifestation: I came in because what started as eating cleaner for the lieutenant track has turned into me cutting meals down to things like black coffee, a protein shake, and a small dinner even on shift days when I know I burned way more than that.
target_item.reason: The doctor is directly asking whether I intentionally restrict how much I eat, even when hungry, because of weight or shape concerns.

patient.answer:
Yeah… yes. I mean, that’s probably the most honest answer.

It started out feeling more reasonable than it probably is now. Like I told myself I was just eating cleaner, being disciplined, trying to stay lean and ready, especially with trying to move toward the lieutenant track. In my head it was tied to being professional and squared away, not just appearance. But over time it’s turned into me cutting things down a lot more than I think I want to admit.

Like there are shift days where I know, objectively, I’ve burned a lot. We’re moving, training, calls, hauling gear, whatever it is. And I’ll still keep it to black coffee in the morning, maybe a protein shake, and then a small dinner later. And I’ll feel hungry, yeah. I’ll feel it. I’m not confused about whether I’m hungry. I just kind of override it because eating more makes me anxious about my weight or how I’ll look.

I’ll tell myself, “You don’t need that much,” or “Just wait until later,” or “You’ll feel better if you keep it tight today.” And sometimes it does feel better mentally for a little while, like I stayed in control. But I also know it’s not really matching what my body probably needs, especially on work days. So… yeah, I am restricting on purpose. I don’t like saying it that directly, but that’s what it is.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits significant concerns about weight and shape, restrictive eating behaviors, and associated distress and social withdrawal, consistent with anorexia nervosa. There is no evidence of recurrent binge eating or compensatory behaviors required for bulimia nervosa.
